speaker: interviewer
text: Hi, thanks for joining. I'm on the infrastructure team, and I'll mostly be asking about backend systems today, with a bit of coding and a couple of questions about how you work.

speaker: candidate
text: Thanks for having me. That sounds good.

speaker: interviewer
text: So, uh, to start us off, how would you, um, design a rate limiter for an internal API that a few hundred services call?

speaker: candidate
text: Just to check, do you mean a limit per calling service, or one global limit for the whole API?

speaker: interviewer
text: Per calling service. Assume each one has its own quota, and the quotas change maybe once a week.

speaker: candidate
text: Okay. Then I'd use a token bucket per service, keyed by the caller's identity from the service mesh. The buckets live in Redis so every instance of the API sees the same count, and each instance keeps a small local cache so most requests don't need a round trip. Quotas come from a config service, since they change so rarely.

speaker: interviewer
text: And if the limiter's state lived in Redis and Redis went down for a minute, what would you want to happen?

speaker: candidate
text: I'd fail open with a conservative local limit on each instance, so internal traffic keeps flowing, and page someone. Failing closed would turn a Redis blip into an outage for every service at once.

speaker: interviewer
text: Right, that's the usual trade, right? Most teams I've worked with land in the same place.

speaker: interviewer
text: Okay, let's switch gears to something more hands-on. Given a stream of log lines, how would you find the ten most frequent error messages in the last hour?

speaker: candidate
text: I'd keep a count per normalized message in a hash map, with a queue of timestamps so I can expire entries older than an hour as new lines arrive. For the top ten I'd keep a small heap, or just sort the counts when someone asks, since there are only a few thousand distinct errors.

speaker: interviewer
text: What's the time complexity of that, and how much memory does it need?

speaker: candidate
text: Each line is constant time to count and expire, and the top ten is k log n with a heap. Memory is linear in the lines inside the window, because of the timestamp queue, plus the distinct messages in the map.

speaker: interviewer
text: Sorry, give me one second, my notes app just froze. Okay, I'm back.

speaker: interviewer
text: Tell me about a time you had to push back on a deadline.

speaker: candidate
text: Last spring we were asked to ship a billing migration in three weeks. I mapped the work and showed that the data backfill alone needed two, with no time left to test. I proposed shipping the new write path on time and backfilling behind a flag the week after, and my manager took that to the product lead.

speaker: interviewer
text: What did you, uh, what did you actually say to your manager?

speaker: candidate
text: I said the date was possible only if we skipped the reconciliation tests, and that I wasn't willing to skip them on money. Then I showed the split plan, so it wasn't just a no.

speaker: interviewer
text: That's a good way to frame it. I've seen people just say no and leave it there.

speaker: interviewer
text: Can you explain the difference between optimistic and pessimistic locking?

speaker: candidate
text: Pessimistic locking takes the lock before touching the row, so nobody else can change it until you commit. Optimistic locking doesn't lock at all. It reads a version number, and the update only succeeds if the version hasn't changed, so you retry on conflict. Optimistic wins when conflicts are rare.

speaker: interviewer
text: Imagine you're building the notification service for a food delivery app. Orders change state every few seconds. How would you get those updates to the customer's phone quickly?

speaker: candidate
text: Order state changes go onto a stream, keyed by order. A notification service consumes it, looks up the customer's devices, and sends a push notification for the important changes, like picked up or arriving. While the app is open, it holds a web socket to a gateway, so the map and the status update in real time.

speaker: interviewer
text: Would you use push for everything, or keep the web socket open, or something else?

speaker: candidate
text: Both. Push when the app is in the background, because the phone kills sockets, and the socket only while the app is open, because it's cheaper and faster than push for every small change.

speaker: interviewer
text: Walk me through a time a production incident was your fault.

speaker: candidate
text: I shipped a config change that set a cache time to live in seconds instead of milliseconds, so every cache entry lived a thousand times longer than intended, and customers saw stale prices for about forty minutes. I rolled it back, wrote the incident review, and owned the fix.

speaker: interviewer
text: How did you, uh, how did you make sure it didn't happen again?

speaker: candidate
text: We changed every duration in our config to carry its unit, like thirty seconds or five hundred milliseconds, and the loader rejects a bare number. Then I added a canary check that compares cache hit rates before and after a config change.

speaker: interviewer
text: So, um, what happens when you type a URL into the browser and press enter? At a high level.

speaker: candidate
text: The browser resolves the name with DNS, opens a TCP connection and does the TLS handshake, then sends the HTTP request. The server answers with HTML, and the browser parses it, fetches the other resources it references, and renders the page.

speaker: interviewer
text: Let me see, where was I on my list. Okay, here.

speaker: interviewer
text: Suppose the log volume from earlier grows ten times overnight, because a new team starts logging every request. What breaks first in your design?

speaker: candidate
text: Memory breaks first. The timestamp queue holds every line in the window, so ten times the lines is ten times the memory. I'd replace the exact queue with per minute buckets of counts, sixty buckets for the hour, which caps memory at the number of distinct messages times sixty, and I'd sample the noisy team's info logs before they reach the counter at all.

speaker: interviewer
text: Describe a time you disagreed with a teammate about a design, and how it got resolved.

speaker: candidate
text: A teammate wanted to shard our job queue by customer from day one. I thought it was premature, because our biggest customer was a tenth of the load. We agreed on a test instead of a debate. We replayed a week of traffic against both designs in staging, the single queue held up with plenty of room, and we wrote down the load at which we'd revisit sharding. A year later we hit that number and did it, and nobody had to argue about it again.

speaker: interviewer
text: Why would you put a message queue between two services instead of having one call the other directly?

speaker: candidate
text: A queue decouples them in time. The producer keeps working when the consumer is slow or down, bursts get smoothed out, and you can add consumers to scale. The cost is that the caller no longer gets an answer back right away, so it fits work that can happen later, like sending email or updating a search index, and not a request where the user is waiting for the result.

speaker: interviewer
text: Okay, great. We're almost out of time. Do you have any questions for me?

speaker: candidate
text: Yes, two. What does the on-call rotation look like for this team, and what's the biggest thing you'd want someone in this role to fix in their first six months?

speaker: interviewer
text: On-call is one week in six, and honestly the biggest thing is our deploy pipeline, it's slow and every team has patched it differently. Thanks again for your time, the recruiter will be in touch this week.

speaker: candidate
text: Thank you, this was fun.
